record.paper_title: A New Paradigm for Scattering Theory of Linear and Nonlinear Waves: Review and Open Problems
record.original_question: Can there be resonances that are purely nonlinear, generated by nonlinear interactions rather than by a linear Hamiltonian, such as long-lived interactions among two or more solitons before they separate or merge? If such lifetimes appear as resonances in scattering, how can they be recovered from the scattering matrix?

evidence.quote: Problem 3 The question above raises the possibility that there are resonances which are purely nonlinear: driven by purely nonlinear interaction terms. How can this happen? Imagine a nonlinearity which has soliton solutions. It can occur that two or more solitons interact for a long time with each other, before separating or merging. The lifetime of such a process will show up as a resonance in the scattering. How can we find it from the Scattering Matrix?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a nonlinear dispersive evolution equation on $\mathbb{R}^n$ (for instance, a nonlinear Schrödinger, Klein–Gordon, or KdV-type equation) that admits soliton solutions and possesses a well-defined scattering theory: there exist wave operators relating solutions of the nonlinear equation, in the distant past and the distant future, to asymptotic configurations consisting of freely propagating radiation together with a finite collection of outgoing solitons. Let $S$ denote the associated nonlinear scattering operator, which maps incoming asymptotic data to outgoing asymptotic data.

A resonance in linear scattering is classically characterized as a pole (or, more generally, a singularity) of the meromorphic continuation of the scattering matrix across the continuous spectrum, with the imaginary part of the pole encoding the inverse lifetime of a metastable state. In the nonlinear setting under consideration, suppose the dynamics exhibits long-lived multi-soliton interaction states: configurations in which two or more solitons remain in close interaction for a long but finite time $T \gg 1$ before either separating into freely propagating solitons or merging, and such that no analogous metastable state exists for the linearization of the equation about the zero solution.

(a) Formulate a precise definition of a "purely nonlinear resonance," i.e., a resonance of the nonlinear scattering process that is not present in, nor inherited from, the linear (Hamiltonian) part of the equation, and that captures the lifetime $T$ of such long-lived multi-soliton interactions.

(b) Determine whether, and under what hypotheses on the nonlinearity, such purely nonlinear resonances can actually occur.

(c) Devise a procedure to extract these resonances and their lifetimes from the nonlinear scattering operator $S$ alone — for example, by identifying suitable singularities, poles, or analytic continuations of $S$ (viewed as a map on appropriate spaces of asymptotic data) whose location encodes the inverse lifetime of the long-lived interacting soliton configurations.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an explicitly open problem in a recent review on scattering theory of nonlinear waves; no resolution or general definition of "purely nonlinear resonance" recoverable from the nonlinear scattering matrix appears in the literature. Related work on multi-soliton interactions exists but does not provide a general answer.

status_evidence.title: A New Paradigm for Scattering Theory of Linear and Nonlinear Waves: Review and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Lists open problems on nonlinear scattering, including resonances of purely nonlinear origin arising from long-lived soliton interactions.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is stated as an open problem in a 2024 review.
